passages.t: The guilt offering, and who keeps what
passages.happening:
“Now this is the law of the guilt offering, which is most holy” (verse 1). It is killed where the burnt offering is killed. The priest sprinkles its blood on all sides of the altar and burns its fat (verses 2-5). “Every male among the priests may eat of it. It must be eaten in a holy place; it is most holy” (verse 6).

“The guilt offering is like the sin offering; the same law applies to both. It belongs to the priest who makes atonement with it” (verse 7).

The priest who offers someone's burnt offering keeps its hide (verse 8). A cooked grain offering belongs to the priest who presents it, and other grain offerings are shared equally among all the sons of Aaron (verses 9-10).
passages.hearers:
The priests' side of the offerings, begun in chapter 6, continues. Chapter 5 told the worshiper when to bring a guilt offering and what to repay. Here the priests learn how to handle it. It is treated like the sin offering: the blood on the altar, the fat burned, the meat eaten by the priests in the courtyard.

Then the passage settles a practical question. Who keeps what? The priest who does the work keeps the hide of a burnt offering, and the baked bread of a grain offering. The rest is shared out equally.

Rules like these may seem dull. But the priests owned no farmland, and these shares were their living. A clear rule, known to everyone, kept the strong from taking more than their part. The story of Eli's sons, who seized what they wanted from worshipers, shows what happened when the rules were ignored (1 Samuel 2:12-17).
passages.later:
God told Aaron why the priests had no fields: “You will have no inheritance in their land, nor will you have any portion among them. I am your portion and your inheritance among the Israelites” (Numbers 18:20).

Paul drew on this pattern for those who serve the church: “In the same way, the Lord has prescribed that those who preach the gospel should receive their living from the gospel” (1 Corinthians 9:14).
passages.asks: The law made sure that those who served at the altar could live, and that none of them could grab. Ask whether the people who serve your church are fairly provided for. And if you handle what belongs to others, ask whether your dealings would stand being known to everyone.

passages.t: The peace offering: thanks, vows and free gifts
passages.happening:
“Now this is the law of the peace offering that one may present to the LORD” (verse 11). There are three kinds.

If it is offered ‘in thanksgiving’, it comes with unleavened cakes and wafers, and with cakes of leavened bread. One of each kind goes to the priest (verses 12-14). The meat “must be eaten on the day he offers it; none of it may be left until morning” (verse 15).

If it is offered for a vow or as a freewill gift, it may be eaten that day and the next. Anything left to the third day must be burned (verses 16-17). If it is eaten then, “it will not be accepted” (verse 18).

Meat that touches anything unclean is burned. “But if anyone who is unclean eats meat from the peace offering that belongs to the LORD, that person must be cut off from his people” (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
The book's teaching on the offerings ends with its most joyful one. Chapter 3 described the peace offering from the worshiper's side. Now we learn why people brought it.

Some brought it to say thank you. A person rescued from sickness, danger or enemies came to the sanctuary, told what God had done, and held a feast. The Hebrew word is todah, thanksgiving. Many of the psalms of thanks grew out of such meals, and may have been sung at them.

Some brought it to keep a vow. A person in trouble promised God an offering if he came through, and afterwards paid it with a feast. And some brought it simply because they wanted to.

The time limits had a kind effect. A whole ox or sheep was far more meat than one family could eat in a day or two. So the rule pushed the giver to invite others: relatives, servants, the Levite, the poor. Thanks, in Israel, was not kept as a private feeling. It was told aloud, and it was shared at a table.

The thanksgiving feast also had leavened bread in it. Leaven was never burned on the altar (2:11), but these loaves were not burned. They were eaten.

Because this meat was holy, it had to be eaten by people who were clean, at the proper time. To eat God's food while unclean was among the gravest wrongs in the chapter. It brought uncleanness into direct touch with what belonged to God.
passages.later:
A psalm ends at just such a feast: “I will offer to You a sacrifice of thanksgiving and call on the name of the LORD. I will fulfill my vows to the LORD in the presence of all His people” (Psalm 116:17-18).

Another calls the rescued to it: “Let them offer sacrifices of thanksgiving and declare His works with rejoicing” (Psalm 107:22).

Jeremiah, facing the ruin of Jerusalem, promised a day when the city would again hear ‘the voices of those bringing thank offerings into the house of the LORD’ (Jeremiah 33:11).

The letter to the Hebrews takes up the thank offering for Christians: “let us continually offer to God a sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips that confess His name” (Hebrews 13:15). At his last supper Jesus “took the bread, gave thanks and broke it” (Luke 22:19). Some scholars think this thanksgiving meal is one of the patterns behind the Lord's Supper; others see Passover as the main background.
passages.hard:
What does it mean to be ‘cut off from his people’?

The phrase comes four times in this chapter and many times in the Torah, always for serious offenses. The text never defines it, and readers have understood it in several ways. Some think it meant being put to death by the community. Others take it as being sent away from the covenant people. Many, among them the ancient rabbis, understood it as a penalty that God himself carried out, not a human court: an early death, the ending of a family line, or being parted from one's ancestors after death.

The strongest evidence points to God as the one who acts. In 20:3 he says of a man who gives a child to Molech, “I will set My face against that man and cut him off from his people”, and he adds that he will do so even if the community looks away. That fits the wrongs named in this chapter. They usually happened out of sight, at home. No court could police them. The penalty left them in the hands of the God who sees.

These notes do not settle the meaning. And the phrase is no warrant for any person or church today to cut someone off.
passages.asks: Israel's thanks took the form of a story told and a meal shared. Ask what God has brought you through that you have never told anyone. And ask whom you could invite to your table, this week, as a way of saying thank you.

passages.t: Fat and blood are not to be eaten
passages.happening:
The LORD tells Moses to say to all Israel, “You are not to eat any of the fat of an ox, a sheep, or a goat” (verse 23). The fat of an animal found dead or torn by wild beasts may be put to other uses, but not eaten (verse 24).

“You must not eat the blood of any bird or animal in any of your dwellings. If anyone eats blood, that person must be cut off from his people” (verses 26-27).
passages.hearers:
These words are addressed to everyone, not to the priests. The rules of the sanctuary reached into every kitchen in Israel.

The rule repeats the last verse of chapter 3 and adds detail. The fat in question is the fat of the three kinds of animal that could be offered on the altar. It was God's share of every sacrifice, so it was not to become ordinary food, even when the animal had not been sacrificed. It could be used for other things. It simply was not eaten.

Blood is forbidden more widely still: the blood ‘of any bird or animal’. The reason is given later in the book. The life of a creature is in its blood, and God has given blood for atonement on the altar (17:11). Blood belongs to God because life does.

So an Israelite family was reminded at ordinary meals, as well as at the altar, that a life had been taken for the food on the table, and that life is God's.
passages.later:
The rule about blood reaches back before Israel existed. God said to Noah, “you must not eat meat with its lifeblood still in it” (Genesis 9:4).

Later in this book God gives the reason: “For the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it to you to make atonement for your souls upon the altar” (Leviticus 17:11). The note on chapter 3:17 sets out how Christians have understood the rule for themselves.
passages.asks: Every meal of meat reminded Israel that a life had been given. Ask whether you receive your food with thanks, or without a thought. And ask what else in your daily life has cost another's labor or life, and how you honor that.

passages.t: The priests' portion, and the summary
passages.happening:
The person who brings a peace offering is to bring God's part ‘with his own hands’ (verse 30). The fat is burned on the altar. The breast is lifted before the LORD as a wave offering and belongs to Aaron and his sons (verses 30-31). The right thigh goes to the priest who offers the blood and the fat (verses 32-33).

God says, “I have given them to Aaron the priest and his sons as a permanent portion from the sons of Israel” (verse 34).

Then the whole section is closed. “This is the law of the burnt offering, the grain offering, the sin offering, the guilt offering, the ordination offering, and the peace offering, which the LORD gave Moses on Mount Sinai” (verses 37-38).
passages.hearers:
The worshiper could not send a servant with the offering. He brought it ‘with his own hands’. As in chapter 1, worship was something a person did, not something done for him at a distance.

The ‘wave offering’ was a gesture. Many scholars think the breast was lifted up before God and not waved from side to side, and some translations call it the elevation offering. It showed that this food was first given to God, and that it then came to the priests from him. God says so: ‘I have given them.’ The priests' food passed through God's hands on its way to their table.

The last two verses sum up seven chapters. They list the offerings and say where the teaching was given: at Mount Sinai. One item in the list has not yet been described, the ‘ordination offering’. It is about to be. In the next chapter Moses ordains Aaron and his sons, and the offerings begin.
passages.later:
The instructions for ordaining the priests were given in Exodus, where the breast and thigh of the ordination ram are set apart in the same way (Exodus 29:26-28).

Deuteronomy names a different set of cuts for the priests: “the shoulder, the jowls, and the stomach” (Deuteronomy 18:3). Some scholars see two periods or traditions here. Rabbinic tradition applied Deuteronomy's rule to animals killed for ordinary food and this chapter's rule to sacrifices. The difference is real, and the text does not explain it.
passages.asks: The priests' share came to them as God's gift, by way of the people's hands. Ask whether you think of what you give to those who serve you in God's name as a favor from you, or as something God gives through you. And ask what you could bring him yourself and not leave to someone else.
